scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Huaconada is a ritual dance of pre-Hispanic origin from the village of Mito.
It represents a fusion of Andean and Spanish elements, serving as a moral and social guide for the community.
In 2010, it was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance occurs annually on the first three days of January.
The huacones represent the former council of elders and hold absolute power in the village during this period.
It is a ritual of moral authority, respect, and fear.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed in the center of the village.
Younger huacones perform circumscribed steps around the elders.
Elders have the freedom to improvise their movements.
Watch for Cuti cuti, Inti Palpoy, Anca Palpoy.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Younger huacones dance in circles around the elders

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is driven by an orchestra directed by the beat of the tinya, a small indigenous drum.
The rhythm is described as a series of different rhythms played to accompany the choreographed and improvised movements.
Listen for the Tinya (small indigenous drum).
The music is defined by the steady, rhythmic beating of the tinya drum, which provides the tempo for the dancers' movements.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performers wear wool hats or 'chuco', serge blankets as capes, black pants, white aprons, wool socks, and 'llanque' sandals.
Masks are made of wood with grotesque features and condor-beak noses.
Whips made of ox hide with wooden handles are carried as symbols of authority.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: The dance is a restricted ritual performed only by men of good conduct and moral integrity; outsiders should observe with respect and not attempt to participate in the ritual authority roles.

scenes.title: Until next time
narration: In the Andean village of Mito, a masked council of elders takes control for three days every January.
